Drop in your documents, ask questions, fine-tune: all from R, free

Source: vignettes/articles/introducing-0-4-0.Rmd
introducing-0-4-0.Rmd

Tejas Patel, October 2026

I wanted to answer questions from a folder of PDFs and web pages without sending them anywhere, and then, if that was not enough, to teach a small model the material. Doing it from R meant stitching together Python libraries, a retriever, a training loop, and a lot of GPU memory arithmetic. So I put the stitching in a package.

dragonfarm 0.4.0 starts from documents rather than from a table. It reaches CRAN in November; until then it installs as a ready-built package from R-universe. Here it is on Costco’s 2024 annual report, all 76 pages of it:

install.packages("dragonfarm", repos = c("https://tejas4patel.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
library(dragonfarm)

docs <- dragon_documents("COST-2024-Annual-Report.pdf", name = "costco-2024")
dragon_ask(docs, "Who is Costco's independent registered public accounting firm?")
#> Costco's independent registered public accounting firm is KPMG LLP, located in Seattle, WA [1].
#>
#> [1]* COST-2024-Annual-Report.pdf, p. 68 › Item 14—Principal Accounting Fees and Services
#> [2]  COST-2024-Annual-Report.pdf, p. 7 › Costco Wholesale Corporation
#> ...

dragon_ask(docs, "What was net cash used in investing activities in fiscal 2024?")
#> Net cash used in investing activities in fiscal 2024 totaled $4,409 million [1].
#>
#> [1]* COST-2024-Annual-Report.pdf, p. 34 › Cash Flows from Investing Activities

Every answer names the page it came from, so you can check it. On thirteen factual questions about the report it got twelve right; on the thirteenth, a total printed inside a map graphic, it said the document does not cover it rather than guessing.

That is the whole first step. PDFs, Word files, HTML, Markdown, spreadsheets, and web pages are read, split into chunks of about 170 words that never cross a heading, and indexed locally with a small embedding model. A question pulls the four most relevant excerpts, puts them in front of a language model with an instruction to answer only from them, and the answer comes back with numbered sources. Nothing leaves your machine, nothing is trained yet, and for a lot of uses this is already the finish line.

The model is picked for the GPU you have. On an 8 GB laptop card that is a 7B model loaded in 4-bit: the first question takes about a minute while it loads, later ones a few seconds. Under 6 GB you get a 1.5B, on a CPU the same, slower. dragon_check() tells you which.

Getting there took more than a reader per file type. That annual report came out of the standard PDF library as two-letter fragments (“Co st co Wh ol es al e”); its cash-flow figures sit pages away from the “(dollars in millions)” note that gives them their unit; its table of contents and page headers look like content. The Word version of the same report hides its sub-headings in italics. Each of those is now handled, and each was found by running a real document through, not by reading the code.

When answering is not enough

Sometimes you want the model to carry the house style, the vocabulary, or the way your team phrases a policy, and not just read it back. That is fine-tuning, and it normally needs a table of prompts and replies that nobody has. dragonfarm writes one from the documents:

qa <- dragon_questions(docs)   # a local model writes questions each chunk can answer
qa                             # every pair kept or rejected, with the reason

The questions are written by the same local model that answers, picked for your GPU (a 7B in 4-bit on an 8 GB card), or by Claude if you pass it as the generator. Filters throw out questions the passage cannot answer, answers that drift from the text, and duplicates. With the 7B writing them, 78 to 87 percent survived on real documents (R’s manuals, the annual report); a small model writing them fares far worse. Then you look at them. The app has a Teach step for this: questions grouped by the chunk they came from, a checkbox each, the rejection reason shown so you can overrule it. The review is the point. Training on unreviewed machine-written pairs is how a small model learns to make its mistakes confident.

dragon_questions_save(qa)
run <- dragon_train(dragon_questions_dataset(qa, docs), "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",
                    hardware = dragon_hardware(load_in_4bit = TRUE),
                    args = dragon_train_args(batch_size = 1, grad_accum = 16, gradient_checkpointing = TRUE),
                    wait = TRUE)
dragon_chat(run, documents = docs)$say("What drove the change in gross margin?")

Every training prompt carries the retrieved excerpts, the same way the model will see them later. On R’s own manuals, a 7B trained this way on the same 8 GB laptop card (overnight, about four hours) stayed exactly as accurate as before and changed only its manner: shorter answers, an excerpt cited every time. Smaller models trained on the same pairs answered more questions too, but they also learned to cite a source for things the source does not say. Fine-tuning is for style once the model is big enough to know when to stop.

In a controlled test on support tickets this mattered more than I expected: the model trained with excerpts in its prompts recalled 89 percent of the policy facts on unseen tickets against 68 percent for a plain fine-tune, and when I edited the policy after training it followed the new text in 88 percent of answers while the plain fine-tune kept repeating the old one. The documents stay the source of truth and can change without retraining.

The app

dragon_app() opens on the Documents step and walks six: Documents, Ask, Teach, Train, Monitor, Try it. Drop files, ask, review, train, watch the loss, compare the tuned model against the base model with both answering from your documents. If you already have a table of prompts and replies, one link switches to that route.

The app, step by step: drop in documents, ask them with sources, review generated questions, train, watch the loss, compare against the base model.

How big a model do you need?

I ran the same tests on four sizes of the same model family, on the same 8 GB card. Before any training, answering from the documents:

Model Costco figures right R questions right Wrong or empty, of 55 Declined the 20 it could not answer
0.5B 17 of 23 19 of 32 14 16
1.5B 19 of 23 28 of 32 6 20
3B 20 of 23 30 of 32 5 20
7B, 4-bit 23 of 23 31 of 32 1 20

The smaller models get plenty right, but they are wrong far more often, and it took work to make them say “the documents do not cover that”: before this release the 0.5B declined none of those questions and made up details about Costco’s executives. After fine-tuning on the manuals the small ones got worse in that one way: the tuned 1.5B said France won the 2022 World Cup and cited the R manual for it. For a fixed format the picture flips: every size, 0.5B included, scored 20 of 20 on ticket-to-JSON after training, and the 0.5B took under three minutes. The details are in Choosing a model size.

What it needs

R, about 3 GB of disk for the Python environment the package sets up on first use, and either an NVIDIA GPU, Apple Silicon, or patience. A 0.5B model trains in a few minutes on a laptop GPU; on an 8 GB card a 7B in 4-bit (QLoRA) takes about 22 minutes for three epochs on a couple of hundred short examples. No GPU at all? dragon_bundle() and dragon_remote() send the run to a free Colab or Kaggle GPU and bring the adapter back.

What to expect, honestly

Retrieval does most of the work and a larger answering model helps more than training does, so the default is to answer first and train second. A small model trained on a few hundred generated pairs learns to cite and to answer in one sentence, but also to answer with confidence when the documents are silent. Questions that need every row of a spreadsheet or every year of a table (“which year had the highest margin?”) are out of reach for excerpt retrieval; ask those in R on the data. Tables inside PDFs flatten into lines of text, scans need OCR first, and numbers inside charts are lost. The numbers above come from a handful of documents, not from yours, and From your documents to your model has the full measurements and the settings behind each one.

The package is MIT licensed. Issues, documents that break it, and pull requests are all welcome at github.com/tejas4patel/dragonfarm; there are a few good first issues to start from.
